contract.note: Reading it as current GPT's incomplete systematic generalisation, tested with arithmetic, is fair because the speaker cites arithmetic studies himself. 'Full mastery' and the 2022 window are the evaluator's choices, but they are ordinary ones.

evidence.note: June 2022 tests of a contemporary GPT model (code-davinci-002): few-shot addition breaks when an equivalent delimited format is used. This directly shows a rule not applied across equivalent forms.
August 2022 preprint: GPT-3 performs poorly out of distribution on copying and addition. This shows failure on unfamiliar instances of simple rules.

Same paper: callable programs and the tutor method improve results. That is assisted performance on finite tests, and GPT-3 with programs still degrades with more digits, so it does not show full mastery.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary 2022 evaluations show contemporary GPT models failing to apply simple arithmetic and copy rules across equivalent formats and out-of-distribution lengths. The assisted gains in e3 do not establish reliable unassisted generalisation. The support condition is met.

contract.note: Reading 'pastiche' as learned stylistic imitation that produces fluent but inappropriate combinations is a fair plain reading. Requiring causal rather than resemblance evidence suits a causal claim.

evidence.note: TruthfulQA shows GPT-3 imitating human misconceptions. That is copying falsehoods found in training text, not producing novel combinations like churro-surgery, which the contract says must be kept separate. The paper itself allows non-imitation causes.
OpenAI's own disclosure that GPT-3 is trained on internet text and fine-tuned on human demonstrations. That makes imitation plausible but does not isolate the cause of the error.

reviews.rationale: No item analyses the churro-surgery output or comparable novel combinations. TruthfulQA concerns imitated misconceptions, a different class of error. The evidence makes imitation plausible but does not settle the causal claim either way.
